The committee said it found no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with or propositioned any of his staffers.
The report said Edwards denied that any of his conduct was intended to be a sexual or romantic advance, and the committee said he cooperated with the investigation.
The Ethics Committee's report was 25 pages long and followed a monthslong investigation opened earlier this year after complaints about Edwards's conduct.

facts.text: Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants who arrive by sea, swimming into the enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla, cannot be subjected to the fast-track/summary deportation procedure applied to people intercepted crossing physical border infrastructure such as fences, and must be processed under more stringent legal procedures.
Tens of thousands of people attempted to cross from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in late July.
Nearly 60,000 people converged on Ceuta on Friday of the previous week, according to Al Jazeera.
A mass border crossing at Ceuta occurred on July 28 and in the days that followed.
Dozens of people drowned or were killed in crowd-related incidents during the Ceuta crossings, according to authorities.
Spanish authorities said at least 67 bodies were recovered after migrants drowned.
European, Spanish and Moroccan authorities attributed the surge in crossings to incorrect information circulating on social media and to human traffickers.
The Supreme Court ruling was issued on July 29.
Social media posts claimed the Supreme Court ruling prevented Spanish authorities from returning migrants who reached Spanish territory by sea.
A Facebook post published on July 13 in Arabic described the Supreme Court ruling as historic and said it prohibited the immediate deportation of irregular migrants.
DW Fact Check assessed the claim that the ruling prohibits immediate deportation of irregular migrants as misleading.
Under Spanish law, authorities may carry out immediate returns of people intercepted while breaching official border infrastructure.
The Supreme Court ruling permits the Spanish government to install physical barriers at sea, and Spain has since installed such barriers.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and other Spanish officials said on July 31 that organized networks had spread inaccurate information about the Supreme Court ruling.
Moroccan authorities denied accusations that they deliberately allowed the crossings and attributed the mass movement to misleading information on social media.

Lorenzo Piccoli, Assistant Professor of Migration Governance at the European University Institute, told DW that in 2015 and 2016 daily arrivals in Europe did not exceed 5,000 to 6,000, compared with 50,000 to 60,000 in a single day in this case.
A Facebook and Instagram page called "Hagra sueta 26" had about 38,000 followers on Facebook and 80,000 on Instagram and posted photographs and videos of people who had swum to Ceuta.
A Facebook group called "haraga maroc" has 12,000 members and includes the phrase "migration to Spain" in its description.

The Spanish newspaper La Razon, citing an intelligence report, reported that social media accounts and groups in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, France and the United States circulated mobilisation messages, logistics information, routes to Ceuta, and advice on passing the maritime barrier at Tarajal.
The intelligence report cited by La Razon stated that the campaign was not centralised and that roles were divided among producing, amplifying, resharing and coordinating content.
A Moroccan woman named Farah from Larache swam more than 5km from Fnideq to Ribera Beach in Ceuta, and a photograph of her raising a victory sign circulated widely.
A video presented as showing a Moroccan man swimming to Ceuta was later shown to have been filmed in El Jadida in western Morocco, and the man posted videos denying any attempt to migrate.

TikTok influencer shot dead during livestream in Mexico

facts.text: Mexican influencer César Gastélum was shot dead while livestreaming on TikTok, according to local authorities.
Gastélum was livestreaming with two friends outside a fast food restaurant in Culiacán, Sinaloa, on Tuesday.
Two men on a motorbike approached the group and one of them shot Gastélum at close range in the head, after which the broadcast ended.
Gastélum had more than half a million followers on TikTok (close to 600,000) and mainly posted comedy videos.
During the livestream, Gastélum and his friends were dressed as delivery drivers, wearing bright orange coats and delivery-style bags, reportedly as part of a challenge for the video.
Initial police reports identified the victim as a delivery worker because of the clothing, before he was identified as Gastélum.
Beauty influencer Valeria Márquez, 23, was shot dead while livestreaming on TikTok at a beauty salon in Zapopan, Jalisco, in May 2025, and her death was investigated as possible femicide.
The shooting occurred in Tres Ríos, Culiacán, on Tuesday evening.
Local media reported Gastélum was around 25 years old.
Police and forensic experts cordoned off the site and are examining cartridge casings and CCTV footage.
No arrests have been made, and the two people on the motorbike left the scene.
TikTok removed the video, though portions of it continued to circulate online.
A security official in Sinaloa confirmed Gastélum's death and said a major security operation was under way.
Local television footage showed soldiers and police at the scene, a commercial plaza near the state prosecutor's office in Culiacán, with forensic investigators collecting evidence.
Culiacán, the capital of Sinaloa, has experienced violence for the past two years amid an internal power struggle within the region's dominant drug cartel.
Two Sinaloa cartel factions, Los Chapitos and La Mayiza, fell out in September 2024.
Gastélum posted pictures on Instagram of his travels, nights out, and poses in front of luxury cars.
One of Gastélum's posts showed him at the grave of Leobardo Aispuro, an influencer known as "El Gordo Peruci".
Aispuro was shot dead in December 2024, and police said the killing may have been linked to rivalry between two factions of the Sinaloa cartel.
Authorities arrested Ramón Ángel Álvarez Ayala, known as "El R-1," in Jalisco in July.
Security Minister Omar García Harfuch described Álvarez Ayala as the head of a criminal cell tied to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.
Investigators say Álvarez Ayala played a role in Márquez's death and financed and directed the November 2025 assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo.

topics.title: Perez Hilton hospitalized after livestream incident

articles.title: Perez Hilton recovering in hospital after reports he self-harmed during livestream
Perez Hilton Hospitalized After Reports He Livestreamed Self-Harm

facts.text: Perez Hilton, real name Mario Lavandeira, a celebrity gossip blogger and podcaster, was hospitalized after reports of self-harm during a TikTok livestream.
Emergency services/police responded to Hilton's home in the Miami area on Tuesday after reports of a man livestreaming acts of self-harm on social media.
The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said an individual had been safely recovered and transported by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue to a local hospital.
The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office statement did not name Hilton.
The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said its Crisis Response Unit and licensed mental health professionals were on scene providing support to the individual's family.
Police said deputies located the residence, spoke with family members present, and confirmed the man was alone inside.
Police said officers decided to tactically disengage while continuing to monitor the situation.
The Sheriff's Office said deputies prioritise de-escalation by creating time, distance and opportunities for communication in incidents involving people in mental health crises.
Hilton's TikTok account was suspended shortly after the livestream.

Hilton's managers, Dante Rusciolelli and Rebekah Kochan, said in a joint statement they were aware of concerning content circulating online involving their client and had not been able to make direct contact with him.
Hilton became known in the early 2000s through his celebrity gossip website.
The name Perez Hilton was chosen as a play on the name Paris Hilton.
Hilton wrote in his 2020 memoir that he had many regrets, including giving people nasty nicknames and being unkind to the children of celebrities.
Hilton has three children via surrogacy and continues to cover showbiz news through his blog, social media and a weekly podcast.
The NBC News video report is dated Aug. 5, 2026 and has a runtime of 35 seconds.

topics.title: Police raid on Starbucks Korea headquarters over 'Tank Day'

articles.title: Police raid Starbucks Korea headquarters over 'Tank Day' fiasco
South Korea: Police raid Starbucks HQ over 'Tank Day' fiasco

facts.text: Police searched Starbucks Korea's national headquarters in Seoul in connection with defamation claims over a marketing campaign, with the company confirming the raid took place on Wednesday.
Starbucks Korea ran a coffee tumbler promotion in May, advertising large to-go cups as "tank tumblers" and referring to "Tank Day," coinciding with the anniversary of the 1980 Gwangju Uprising.
Shinsegae Group operates Starbucks in South Korea.
Shinsegae apologised publicly for the marketing campaign.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung criticized the campaign, saying it insulted the victims and the struggle of Gwangju residents.
A Shinsegae Group spokesman said the raid was part of an ongoing investigation.
Police told the Yonhap news agency they were seeking evidence that executives knowingly trivialized the 1980 killings in Gwangju.
Promotional material for the tumbler used the phrase "tak on the table!", with "tak" being the word used in a 1987 police statement about the death of a student activist in custody.
On May 18, 1980, South Korea's military junta suppressed a pro-democracy protest in the city of Gwangju, and at least 165 civilians were killed when the army deployed tanks.
Starbucks withdrew the "Tank Day" promotion and said it was unintentional.
Civic groups filed a criminal complaint against Starbucks, asking police to investigate the company for defaming victims of the military dictatorship.
Shinsegae Group said it conducted an internal investigation into the campaign and concluded the mistake was unintentional.
Starbucks Korea said its internal investigation found no evidence of wrongdoing.
Shinsegae Group said the team that planned the promotion did not identify the connection to the historical event, and that upper management also did not identify it.
Starbucks Korea said its internal inquiry was limited because it could not require employees involved in planning the promotion to provide their phones.
Starbucks stores across South Korea closed for half a day in June so staff could attend history lessons.
Shinsegae said the controversy led to a decline in Starbucks sales in South Korea.
Shinsegae dismissed the chief executive of Starbucks Korea.
Shinsegae Group chairman Chung Yong-jin and Starbucks Korea CEO Son Jung-hyun resigned after the public apology.
South Korea's interior ministry announced a government-level boycott of Starbucks, and the opposition leader held up a Starbucks cup during a speech while accusing the government of overreach.
South Korea is Starbucks' third-largest market after the United States and China.

topics.title: South Dakota Democrat exits Senate race

articles.title: South Dakota Democrat exits Senate race, clears way for independent
South Dakota Senate Democrat drops out, leaving independent candidate to run against Rounds

facts.text: Julian Beaudion, a Democratic candidate for a U.S. Senate seat in South Dakota, withdrew from the race, announcing on a Tuesday that he was suspending his campaign.
According to the article, Beaudion is the third Democrat to exit a Senate race after his party urged him to step aside in favor of an independent candidate.
Beaudion's withdrawal leaves independent candidate Brian Bengs and Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) as the remaining candidates in the South Dakota Senate race.
In a statement posted on X, Beaudion said his family had experienced a house fire and financial hardship.
Beaudion said that after the fire, an opponent and people associated with that opponent made threats intended to pressure him to leave the race.
Beaudion said the mental and physical safety of his family was his priority.
Beaudion said he was not endorsing either Bengs or Rounds.
Bengs is a retired U.S. Air Force lieutenant colonel.
Beaudion previously served as a South Dakota State Trooper.
Bengs said in a statement that he would seek Beaudion's input on issues facing South Dakotans and described Beaudion as a patriot.
Bengs said that the most important goal was retiring Mike Rounds.
Bengs described himself as a small business owner, a 13-year State Trooper, and a community leader in Sioux Falls.
President Trump won South Dakota by nearly 30 percentage points in 2024.
Rounds has held his Senate seat since 2015.
The Cook Political Report rates Rounds's seat as "solid Republican."
